questions.question:
In the context of DBMS, consider the two sets [latex]\mathbf{T}[/latex] and [latex]\mathbf{S}[/latex] given below.

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline \quad\quad\quad\textbf{T} & \quad\quad\quad\textbf{S} \\ \hline \text{I: Logical schema} & \text{L: Views} \\ \text{II: Physical schema} & \text{M: File organization and indexes} \\ \text{III: External schema} & \text{N: Relations} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

Which one of the following is the correct match from [latex]\mathbf{T}[/latex] to [latex]\mathbf{S}[/latex] ?
questions.explanation:
Matching each schema level in the three-tier DBMS architecture to what it describes:

- Logical schema (I): describes the overall logical structure of the database for the whole community of users — this is exactly what relations (N) capture.
- Physical schema (II): describes how data is actually stored at the lowest level — file organization and indexes (M).
- External schema (III): describes a customized, user-specific way of seeing part of the data — exactly what views (L) provide.

Answer: I-N, II-M, III-L

questions.question: In a relational data model, which one of the following statements is TRUE?

options.A: A relation with only two attributes is always in BCNF.
options.B: If all attributes of a relation are prime attributes, then the relation is in BCNF.
options.C: Every relation has at least one non-prime attribute.

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Relation R(A, B): the only possible non-trivial FDs are [latex]A\rightarrow B[/latex] or [latex]B\rightarrow A[/latex]. In each case the left side is a key, so R is always in BCNF [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- All attributes prime guarantees 3NF, not BCNF (e.g. [latex]AB\rightarrow C,\ C\rightarrow B[/latex]) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- A relation can have no non-prime attribute (e.g. all attributes form the key) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- BCNF decomposition does not always preserve FDs [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: A relation with only two attributes is always in BCNF

questions.question:
Consider the following partial Schedule S involving two transactions T1 and T2. Only the read and the write operations have been shown. The read operation on data item P is denoted by read(P) and the write operation on data item P is denoted by write(P).

Suppose that the transaction T1 fails immediately after time instance 9. Which one of the following statements is correct?

options.A: T2 must be aborted and then both T1 and T2 must be re-started to ensure transaction atomicity
options.B: Schedule S is non-recoverable and cannot ensure transaction atomicity
options.C: Only T2 must be aborted and then re-started to ensure transaction atomicity
options.D: Schedule S is recoverable and can ensure atomicity and nothing else needs to be done

questions.explanation:
T2 reads A (time 7) after T1 wrote it (time 2), and T2 commits at time 8 before T1 commits.

When T1 fails, T2 has already committed using a value of A that must be rolled back. Its effects cannot be undone, so S is non-recoverable.

Answer: Schedule S is non-recoverable and cannot ensure transaction atomicity

questions.question:
Consider the following read-write schedule [latex] S [/latex] over three transactions [latex] T_1, T_2 [/latex], and [latex] T_3 [/latex], where the subscripts in the schedule indicate transaction IDs:

[latex] S: r_1(z) ; w_1(z) ; r_2(x) ; r_3(y) ; w_3(y) ; r_2(y) ; w_2(x) ; w_2(y) ; [/latex]

Which of the following transaction schedules is/are conflict equivalent to [latex] S [/latex] ?
questions.explanation:
Conflicting pairs (same item, different transactions, at least one write):
- z: only T1 uses it [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T1 has no conflict with anyone.
- x: only T2 uses it.
- y: [latex]r_3(y),w_3(y)[/latex] come before [latex]r_2(y),w_2(y)[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T3 must come before T2.

So any serial order with T3 before T2 is conflict equivalent, and T1 can be anywhere: [latex]T_1T_3T_2,\;T_3T_2T_1,\;T_3T_1T_2[/latex].
[latex]T_1T_2T_3[/latex] puts T2 before T3 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] not equivalent.

Answer: [latex]T_1T_3T_2[/latex], [latex]T_3T_2T_1[/latex], [latex]T_3T_1T_2[/latex]

Consider an Entity-Relationship (ER) model in which entity sets E1 and E2 are connected by an m : n relationship R12. E1 and E3 are connected by a 1 : n (1 on the side of E1 and n on the side of E3) relationship R13.

E1 has two single-valued attributes a11 and a12 of which a11 is the key attribute. E2 has two single-valued attributes a21 and a22 of which a21 is the key attribute. E3 has two single-valued attributes a31 and a32 of which a31 is the key attribute. The relationships do not have any attributes.

If a relational model is derived from the above ER model, then the minimum number of relations that would be generated if all the relations are in 3NF is _______.
questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- E1(a11, a12), E2(a21, a22): one relation each
- R12 is m:n: needs its own relation (a11, a21)
- R13 is 1:n: add a11 as a foreign key in E3(a31, a32, a11), no separate table

Total = 4

Answer: 4

Suppose R1(A, B) and R2(C, D) are two relation schemas. Let r1 and r2 be the corresponding
relation instances. B is a foreign key that refers to C in R2. If data in r1 and r2 satisfy referential
integrity constraints, which of the following is ALWAYS TRUE?
questions.explanation:
Referential integrity: every B value in r1 must appear as a C value in r2. So [latex]\Pi_B(r_1)\subseteq\Pi_C(r_2)[/latex], i.e. [latex]\Pi_B(r_1)-\Pi_C(r_2)=\phi[/latex].

Equality need not hold (r2 may have C values nobody refers to).

Answer: [latex]\Pi_B(r_1)-\Pi_C(r_2)=\phi[/latex]

questions.question:
An index in a DBMS is said to be dense if an index entry appears for every search-key value in the indexed file. Otherwise it is called a sparse index. Consider the following two statements.

[latex]\text{S1}[/latex]: A hash index must be a dense index
[latex]\text{S2}[/latex]: A [latex]B^{+}[/latex] tree index can be a sparse index

Which one of the following options is correct?
questions.explanation:
S1 (hash index must be dense): A hash index computes a bucket location directly from the key via a hash function; there is no notion of "sorted order" to allow skipping entries the way a sparse index can, so a hash index inherently needs a separate index entry pointing to the data for every distinct search-key value. True.

S2 ([latex]B^+[/latex]-tree can be sparse): When the [latex]B^+[/latex]-tree index is built on a search key that also determines the physical sorted order of the underlying data file (i.e. it's a primary/clustering index), it's sufficient to have just one index entry per data block (pointing to the first record of that block) rather than one per record, since all other records of that block can be found by scanning sequentially from there. This makes a sparse [latex]B^+[/latex]-tree index entirely feasible. True.

Answer: Both S1 and S2 are true.

Consider a database table T containing two columns X and Y each of type integer. After the creation of the table, one record (X=1,Y=1) is inserted in the table.

Let MX and MY denote the respective maximum values of X and Y among all records in the table at any point in time. X = 7: Y = [latex]2^7-1=127[/latex]

questions.question:
Given the following two statements:
S1: Every table with two single-valued attributes is in 1NF, 2NF, 3NF and BCNF
S2 : AB[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]C, D[latex]\rightarrow[/latex] E, E[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]C is a minimal cover for the set of functional dependencies AB[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]C, D[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]E, AB[latex]\rightarrow[/latex] E,E[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]C.
Which one of the following is CORRECT?

options.A: S1 is TRUE and S2 is FALSE
options.B: Both S1 and S2 are TRUE.
options.C: S1 is FALSE and S2 is TRUE.
options.D: Both S1 and S2 are FALSE.

Checking each statement:

- S2: in the given set, AB [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] C is redundant (AB [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] E [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] C). A minimal cover is AB [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] E, D [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] E, E [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] C. The proposed cover drops AB [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] E, which cannot be derived from it [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] FALSE.

questions.question:
Consider the following relational schema along with all the functional dependencies that hold on them.

[latex] R1(A, B, C, D, E): \{ D \to E, EA \to B, EB \to C \} [/latex]
[latex] R2(A, B, C, D): \{ A \to D, A \to B, C \to A \} [/latex]

Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE?
questions.explanation:
[latex]R1(A,B,C,D,E)[/latex]: [latex]\{D\to E,\ EA\to B,\ EB\to C\}[/latex]. Computing candidate keys: [latex]\{A,D\}^+[/latex]: [latex]D\to E[/latex] gives [latex]\{A,D,E\}[/latex]; then [latex]EA\to B[/latex] gives [latex]\{A,B,D,E\}[/latex]; then [latex]EB\to C[/latex] gives all of [latex]\{A,B,C,D,E\}[/latex]. So [latex]\{A,D\}[/latex] is the (only, minimal) candidate key.
Check [latex]D\to E[/latex] against 3NF: is [latex]D[/latex] a superkey? No ([latex]D[/latex] alone only reaches [latex]\{D,E\}[/latex]). Is [latex]E[/latex] a prime attribute (part of some candidate key)? No (the only key is [latex]\{A,D\}[/latex], which doesn't include [latex]E[/latex]). Since neither condition holds, this FD violates 3NF. R1 is NOT in 3NF.

[latex]R2(A,B,C,D)[/latex]: [latex]\{A\to D,\ A\to B,\ C\to A\}[/latex]. [latex]\{C\}^+[/latex]: [latex]C\to A[/latex] gives [latex]\{A,C\}[/latex]; then [latex]A\to D,A\to B[/latex] gives all of [latex]\{A,B,C,D\}[/latex]. So [latex]\{C\}[/latex] alone is the candidate key.
Check [latex]A\to D[/latex]: is [latex]A[/latex] a superkey? No ([latex]A[/latex] alone reaches [latex]\{A,B,D\}[/latex], missing [latex]C[/latex]). Is [latex]D[/latex] prime? No (key is just [latex]\{C\}[/latex]). This FD also violates 3NF. R2 is NOT in 3NF.

Answer: R1 is NOT in 3NF; and R2 is NOT in 3NF.

questions.question:
Consider a relational schema [latex] team(name, city, owner) [/latex], with functional dependencies [latex]\{ name \to city [/latex], [latex] name \to owner \} [/latex] .

The relation [latex] team [/latex] is decomposed into two relations, [latex] t_1(name, city) [/latex] and [latex] t_2(name, owner) [/latex]. Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE?

options.A: The relation [latex] team [/latex] is NOT in BCNF.
options.B: The relations [latex] t_1 [/latex] and [latex] t_2 [/latex] are in BCNF.
options.C: The decomposition constitutes a lossless join.

questions.explanation:
[latex]team(name,city,owner)[/latex] with [latex]name\to city,\ name\to owner[/latex]. Since [latex]name[/latex] alone functionally determines every other attribute, [latex]name[/latex] is already a candidate key of [latex]team[/latex] — and since every FD's left-hand side ([latex]name[/latex]) is already a superkey, [latex]team[/latex] is already in BCNF (and hence also in 3NF) even before decomposing. So both "team is NOT in BCNF" and "team is NOT in 3NF" are false.

Decomposing into [latex]t_1(name,city)[/latex] and [latex]t_2(name,owner)[/latex]: in each projection, [latex]name[/latex] remains a key (it determines the sole remaining attribute), so both [latex]t_1[/latex] and [latex]t_2[/latex] are trivially in BCNF. True.

For losslessness, the common attribute of the decomposition is [latex]name[/latex], and [latex]name\to city[/latex] (i.e. [latex]name[/latex] alone determines all of [latex]t_1[/latex]) — satisfying the standard lossless-join test ([latex]R_1\cap R_2[/latex] is a superkey of at least one of the two pieces). True.

Answer: t1 and t2 are in BCNF; and the decomposition is lossless.
